**The Quiet Chaos of Being Alive**

There’s a strange, almost sacred rhythm to the way time moves when you’re not paying attention. One moment, you’re a child staring at the ceiling fan, convinced it’s a portal to another world. The next, you’re an adult staring at the same fan, wondering if it’s time to replace the lightbulb. Life, in its infinite and infuriating way, keeps turning, whether you’re ready or not.

I’ve been thinking a lot about the weight of small moments lately. The kind that don’t register as important until years later, when you realize they were the threads that held everything together. Like the way my mother’s hands smelled like cinnamon and dish soap when she tucked me in at night, or how my father’s laughter always came in bursts, like he couldn’t contain it. Those details are gone now, or at least, they’re fading. The scent of cinnamon is just a spice in a jar, and my father’s laugh is a memory that flickers like a dying bulb.

Grief isn’t linear. It’s not a straight line from sorrow to acceptance. It’s more like a labyrinth where you keep circling back to the same sharp turns, wondering if you’ll ever find the exit. Some days, it’s a dull ache in your chest, like you’ve swallowed a stone. Other days, it’s a sudden, violent storm—tears you didn’t see coming, anger that rises like bile. And then there are the days when it’s just… quiet. A numbness so deep it feels like floating underwater, where sound is muffled and everything moves in slow motion.

I wonder if this is what getting older *really* means—not the gray hairs or the aches in your knees, but the way your heart starts to feel like a museum exhibit. You walk past the glass cases of your past, pointing at moments like, *“Here’s where I fell in love,”* or *“This is the day everything changed,”* but the labels feel hollow. The emotions are still there, but they’re behind glass now, untouchable.

There’s a kind of beauty in that, though. In the way we curate our own lives, even as they slip through our fingers. We take photos, write journals, save ticket stubs from concerts we’ll never hear again. We do it because we’re afraid of forgetting, but also because we’re afraid of *remembering too much*. What if the past is just a ghost story we tell ourselves to make the present feel less lonely?

I’ve been reading a lot of poetry lately. Not the kind that’s taught in schools—dense, academic, full of allusions—but the kind that feels like a whisper in the dark. Poetry that doesn’t explain itself, that just *is*. Like Mary Oliver’s *“Wild Geese,”* where she writes, *“You do not have to be good. / You do not have to walk on your knees / for a hundred miles through the desert, repenting.”* It’s a permission slip, a release. You don’t have to earn your place in the world. You just have to exist, and that’s enough.

That’s the thing about being alive—it’s exhausting, but it’s also the only thing that makes sense. Even when it doesn’t. Even when the world feels like it’s on fire and no one’s holding the hose. You keep going because what else is there? To stop would be to admit defeat, and defeat is just another word for giving up on the miracle of being here at all.

I think about the people I’ve lost. Not just in death, but in life—the friends who drifted away, the lovers who became strangers, the versions of myself I left behind in different cities, different jobs, different versions of my own story. Where do they go? Are they still out there, living parallel lives, or do they dissolve like sugar in water, leaving only a faint sweetness behind?

Sometimes, I imagine time as a river. Not a calm, gentle stream, but a wild, unpredictable thing—swollen with rain, carving new paths through the earth, eroding the banks of who we were yesterday. We try to dam it up, to control it, to make it hold still so we can take a picture. But the river doesn’t care. It keeps moving, dragging us along whether we’re ready or not.

And maybe that’s the secret. Maybe the point isn’t to resist the current, but to learn how to float. To trust that even when you’re not paddling, the water will carry you somewhere. Maybe not where you planned, but somewhere. Somewhere new.

I don’t know if I believe in an afterlife. I don’t know if I believe in fate, or destiny, or any of the grand narratives we tell ourselves to make sense of the chaos. But I do believe in the quiet persistence of life—the way a dandelion pushes through a crack in the sidewalk, the way a song you haven’t heard in years can suddenly make your chest tighten. I believe in the stubborn, irrational hope that things will get better, even when they don’t. Even when they can’t.

Maybe that’s all we have. Not answers, not guarantees, but the stubborn, ridiculous belief that it’s worth waking up tomorrow and trying again. Worth loving, worth losing, worth the slow unraveling of everything we thought we knew.

I’m sitting here now, listening to the hum of the refrigerator, the distant sound of traffic, the occasional chirp of a bird outside my window. It’s an ordinary moment. A Tuesday, maybe. Or a Thursday. The days blur together like watercolors left in the rain. But in this ordinary moment, there’s a kind of magic. The magic of being alive, of being *here*, even when it doesn’t feel like enough.

And that’s enough. For now.
